# Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka (Ja 540)

**ID:** Ja 540  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul5.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Suvaṇṇasāmajātaka* (Ja 540, PTS Jātaka VI 68ff.), commonly known as the *Sāma-jātaka*, is one of the celebrated "last ten" great jātakas (*Mahānipāta*) [Appleton 2010; Collins 2016; Cabezon 2017]. In the Theravāda tradition, it is associated with the Bodhisatta's perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) and the virtue of supporting one's parents [Appleton 2010; Hazra 1994]. The narrative frame (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha recounts the story in response to a monk who was criticized by his peers for using alms to sustain his aged, destitute parents [Wilson, Buddhism and Family].

In the core narrative, two former deities of the Brahma-world marry without carnal desire and adopt the ascetic life, conceiving a son virginally without sexual intercourse [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities; Cabezon 2017; Nyanaponika, Hecker, Bodhi 2003]. Their son Sāma (the Bodhisatta) dutifully provides for them after they are both blinded by snake venom [Appleton 2010; Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. While drawing water at the river, Sāma is fatally wounded by a poisoned arrow and laments not his own death, but that he can no longer serve his blind parents [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. The story is also cited elsewhere in Pali literature, such as in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.4.6).

The text has left a prominent imprint across Buddhist art, liturgy, and scholarship. Scenes from the jātaka appear on Sri Lankan festival gateways (*toraṇa*) and in eighteenth-century Mon murals in Thailand [Appleton 2010; Collins 2016]. In Cambodian chanted leporellos, vernacular verse compositions preserve the dramatic laments of both Sāma and his mother [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism]. In nineteenth-century scholarship, Eugène Burnouf prepared an extensive 449-page unpublished translation of a Burmese *nissaya* commentary on the text [Lopez 1995].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels: Ja 532 Soṇanandajātaka; Ja 503 Sattigumbajātaka; Ja 547 Vessantarajātaka
- Mentioned in: Mil 5.4.6 Mettābhāvanānisaṁsapañha

**Sources**

- [Lopez 1995] Donald S. Lopez, ed., Curators of the Buddha: The Study of Buddhism Under Colonialism (1995) — Noted Burnouf's unpublished translation of the Burmese nissaya on the text.
- [Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist felicities] Steven Collins, Nirvana and other Buddhist Felicities — Discussed virginal conception of the child by human ascetics without intercourse.
- [Nyanaponika, Hecker, Bodhi 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Cited the past life where two children born from the Brahma-world marry without sensual desire and become ascetics.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Outlined the Bodhisatta caring for blind parents, perfection of mettā, and modern toraṇa depictions.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Noted the association of Suvaṇṇasāma with mettā-pāramī in the Cariyāpiṭaka tradition.
- [Collins 2016] Steven Collins, Readings of the Vessantara Jātaka (2016) — Noted the inclusion of the jātaka in the last ten and its depiction in Mon monastery murals.
- [Cabezon 2017] José Ignacio Cabezón, Sexuality in Classical South Asian Buddhism (2017) — Provided the PTS volume and page reference (PTS 6: 68–) and noted celibate ascetic conception.
- [Walker, Unfolding Buddhism] Trent Walker, Unfolding Buddhism: Communal Scripts, Localized Translations, and the Work of the Dying in Cambodian Chanted Leporellos — Detailed the narrative of the parents blinded by snake venom, Sāma shot with an arrow, and Cambodian chanted laments.
- [Wilson, Buddhism and Family] Liz Wilson, Buddhism and Family — Described the preface narrative of the monk who supported his starving parents with alms.
